mainEntity.name: Is it normal to see the metal implant through the gum?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is common to see the healing abutment — a small cylindrical component placed above the gum — following implant surgery. This is intentional and designed to shape the surrounding gum tissue. However, if you can see the threaded titanium implant fixture itself, this may indicate gum recession or tissue change that warrants clinical review. Your dental team can examine the site and advise whether what you are seeing is expected or requires further assessment.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take for gum tissue to heal around a dental implant?

acceptedAnswer.text: Initial gum tissue healing typically occurs within two to four weeks following implant surgery, though complete tissue maturation can take longer. The overall implant integration process — osseointegration — generally takes between six weeks and six months depending on factors including bone quality, implant location, and individual health. Your clinician will monitor healing at scheduled review appointments and advise when you are ready to progress to the next stage of treatment.

mainEntity.name: Can stress affect dental implant healing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some research suggests that psychological stress may influence the body's immune response and bone healing capacity, potentially affecting osseointegration. Elevated cortisol levels associated with chronic stress have been linked in some studies to altered inflammatory responses. While this remains an area of ongoing research and individual outcomes vary, supporting your general health and wellbeing during the healing period is a sensible and clinically reasonable approach. Speak with your dental team if you have specific concerns.

mainEntity.name: What is peri-implantitis and how does it affect the gum around an implant?

acceptedAnswer.text: Peri-implantitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the soft tissue and bone surrounding a dental implant, caused primarily by bacterial plaque accumulation. It can lead to gum inflammation, recession, and progressive bone loss around the implant if left unaddressed. Early signs may include redness, swelling, and bleeding around the implant site. Maintaining excellent oral hygiene and attending regular dental check-ups are key preventative measures. If peri-implantitis is suspected, a clinical assessment will determine the most appropriate management approach.

mainEntity.name: Should a dental implant feel loose at any stage during healing?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. While some very minor movement during the very earliest stages of healing may occur, a dental implant should not feel noticeably loose or mobile. If you experience any sensation of movement, looseness, or instability around the implant site, you should contact your dental practice promptly. This may indicate that osseointegration has not progressed as expected or that there is an issue with the healing component that requires clinical assessment.

mainEntity.name: What should I eat during dental implant healing?

acceptedAnswer.text: In the initial post-operative period, a soft diet is generally recommended to avoid placing pressure or mechanical stress on the healing implant site. Suitable options typically include soft foods such as soups, yoghurt, mashed vegetables, eggs, and fish. Hard, crunchy, or chewy foods should be avoided near the implant site until your dental team confirms that healing has progressed sufficiently. Your clinician will provide specific dietary guidance tailored to your procedure and healing progress.
